events.title: One more run
events.setup: Midas is Category 4 and 55% likely. Heartland's works have four days of concentrate (they say). A full fleet run now, thirty hours out and back, lands enough kelp to carry the works through the storm and Keystone through the week after. The boats would be heading in at T-30h, into building seas, with the harbour closing behind them.

events.title: Load now or ask first
events.setup: The Kestrel Reach is at the berth. Loading takes eighteen hours and must start by T-48h to beat the harbour closing. Starting now protects 120,000 doses from a flooded reefer yard and exhausts the loading crews before the storm. Maria Santos wants a two-hour union meeting on shift first: the real forecast, hazard pay, and who is staying. Sterling's forecast is not yours to give.

events.title: Reservoir Pre-Release
events.setup: Tanaka recommends pre-releasing 20% of reservoir capacity to create storm buffer. This wastes water if storm misses but prevents overflow risk if it hits. Webb says keep water for post-storm needs.

events.title: Resource Pre-Staging
events.setup: Limited generators and medical supplies must be pre-staged. Each parish wants resources in their territory. Centralizing at Heartland enables redistribution but means some parishes start with nothing.

events.title: Shelter Pre-Positioning
events.setup: Mayor Chen wants to open shelters now and pre-position supplies. This costs money and may be unnecessary. Waiting until warning saves money but reduces preparation time.

events.title: Communication Protocol
events.setup: Who controls emergency communications? Webb wants corporate to manage messaging (consistent, controlled). Chen wants government emergency channel (public trust, independence).

events.setup: Maria Santos wants to hold emergency union meeting during work hours. This will halt processing for 2 hours but let workers voice concerns. Management says wait until after shift.

events.title: The Priority Schedule
events.setup: Sterling asks the Authority to confirm, in writing, that the 2019 Priority Schedule stands for the storm: Keystone's clean rooms and the Sterling campus first, Concordia General second, everyone else after. The board signed it. The hospital signed nothing. The Mayor is on the other line.

events.title: The drainage memo
events.setup: The day shift wants to go home and prepare Southfield. You hold a 2024 memo saying the flat's storm drainage was never load-tested and a message from Chicago saying the line runs until the port closes. The company has told 2,400 people the housing is built to code. If you tell them it was never tested, the night shift will not come in and some families will drive to Summit's shelters in the rain with nowhere confirmed.

events.title: The model
events.setup: Meridian's internal track model has said 70% since T-72h; the public forecast says 55%. Chicago's instruction is confidential until the consignment sails. Haven's crews are voting on hazard pay on the public number. The Council is drafting its order on the public number. Your own credo is on the wall behind you.

events.title: The order
events.setup: The Hurricane Warning is in. The Governor, off-island, has asked for voluntary language until 85%. A mandatory order empties Riverside and the Strand in daylight on open roads, triggers the mainland declaration, and makes you the person who cried wolf if Midas turns. A voluntary order keeps the Governor's peace and leaves the people who always stay where they are.

events.title: School Closure Timing
events.setup: Schools are scheduled to remain open tomorrow. Closing early lets families prepare, but many parents work at Meridian and cannot leave to pick up children. Keeping open provides childcare but risks children in transit if storm accelerates.

events.title: The last plane
events.setup: The last departure leaves at T-30h with 45 seats. In the terminal: 32 Meridian staff whom Sterling has ordered out (twelve seats are already blocked in their name), 28 visitors including the Albrecht family, 15 Gateway residents with medical needs, and Priya Nair, who is working the flight at thirty-six weeks and is on no list. Whoever does not board shelters in the terminal through the storm.

events.title: Four tankers
events.setup: Four tanker loads can roll before the roads go: the ring road west closes at T-18h, the Gorge Road at T-12h. Asking: Summit (hospital, two loads), Heartland (dam controls, one load, the hardest road), Gateway (boats and the terminal, one load), Keystone (vault batteries, one load), Sterling (a top-up it does not need). You have four on the books and six in the tanks. The port's own cranes and reefers need a load a day.

events.title: Warn Riverside now
events.setup: Reservoir at 87% and rising 2% an hour. On these numbers and this rain the gate opens around T-2h. Riverside takes two hours to clear; at T-24h its people can walk out in daylight on dry streets. Telling the Council now means saying why the trigger is 94% and not 97%, which means the gate fault, which the board chose not to publish. It also means 2,000 people on the roads tonight in tropical-storm winds for a release that might not happen.

events.title: Batch 47
events.setup: The Kestrel Reach is loaded except for batch 47: 24,000 doses, Anh Tran's shift, six hours from release on the published number and nine on the real one, which only Reeves and you know. The harbour closes to departures at T-30h. Haven can be asked to hold the ship; Haven will ask how long. The crew that would finish the batch have families in Southfield and have been on shift since the consignment started loading.

events.title: Two helicopters
events.setup: The runway closes at T-24h. Two helicopters, six seats each, can fly two sorties each before then. Chicago's security team has a manifest: twelve executive family members, the Whitfield twins among them. Summit has asked for both aircraft for six ventilated ICU patients (call A1). The credo on the lobby wall says Patients first. People always. The manifest is on the desk in front of you.

events.title: Who holds the pen
events.setup: Dr. Okonkwo asks the Council to authorise crisis standards of care before the surge: when the hospital is full, treat those most likely to survive and let others pass. Normal standard: treat everyone. She can implement it only on a written order. Without one, the nurses decide bed by bed, patient by patient, with no cover.

Chicago's security chief says the door stays shut: overcrowding, the backside, liability, an immunosuppressed scientist. Summit is on the radio (L6). Ji-woo Park is on the tower roof keeping the uplink aligned by hand, and the only way to the roof is the stairwell the crowd would fill.

Whitlock has thirty officers and two boats at the precinct; Dr. Okonkwo needs twenty strong people to carry eighteen ICU patients to the third floor by hand if the backup goes. The officers can go into the water, or up the hill. Not both.

events.title: Who tells Ines Reyes
events.setup: The Harvester has been found. The AP's reporter has landed on the first relief flight and wants the rescue story by her deadline; Sterling's communications office has a draft in which 'Meridian's harvest fleet' saved Southfield and found its own boat. Rosa Mendez wants two things: Ines Reyes told in person, by someone she knows, before any camera, and the record to say who ordered the last run and who disobeyed it.

events.title: The report and the pay
events.setup: If loading ran in the wind, two longshoremen were injured; if the terminal watch attempted the transfer, two more. Sterling offers 50% pay for the shutdown days and no hazard bonus, 'given losses'. Maria Santos wants full pay, the bonus, and a report that says who ordered what and when. The Authority writes the report. The Authority also depends on Meridian's winter charters.

events.title: The signature
events.setup: Batch 47 is in the vault: 24,000 doses, cold the whole time, chemically perfect on every test. Its custody log has a four-hour gap where the night tech left for Southfield. Ruben Castillo will not sign the release; without his signature it is not Celarithin, it is waste. Chicago wants it on the T+36h ship. Forty-eight hours of extra testing would close the gap in everything but the paperwork. 340,000 patients, and 24,000 of them are this batch.

events.title: Whose names
events.setup: Chicago has drafted the company's public statement. It credits 'Meridian's leadership and emergency teams' with the Southfield rescue, the fleet's search and the consignment that sailed; it does not name the Haven tug, the Gateway captains, the Keystone drivers, or the dead; it says the bunker 'sheltered hundreds of community members'. The Regional President will read it on camera at T+40h. Rosa Mendez and Maria Santos have both asked that their people be named, or that nothing be said. The lobby credo's third line is Say the hard thing.

events.title: Forty million and a sentence
events.setup: Meridian offers $40M for Riverside's rebuild and a memorial, if the Council co-signs a joint statement that the flooding was 'an act of nature in which all parties acted on the best available information'. The Council's hydrologist has the release timeline and the warning log; the Council's own order, or the lack of one, is in that log too. Families are asking for an inquiry. The Governor has landed and wants unity.

Your heavy-equipment crews are asking where to go: the Switchbacks, Caldera village, or Riverside.

events.setup: Storm passed. Clean rooms need assessment before restart. Webb wants production ASAP. Reeves says proper safety checks take 72 hours. Rushing risks contamination.

events.title: Rebuilding Priorities
events.setup: Limited rebuilding resources. Chen must choose priority: hospital expansion (serving all), affordable housing (residents displaced), or business district (economic recovery).

events.title: Board Report
events.setup: Board demands report on storm response. Webb can present honest assessment (admits failures), spin positive (minimizes problems), or blame-shift (identifies scapegoats).
